questions.question: What exactly is a data race in Go?
questions.title: The precise Go data-race definition
questions.direct_answer: A Go data race exists when concurrent goroutines perform conflicting accesses to the same memory location—at least one is a write—and those operations are not ordered by happens-before, unless the accesses are synchronized atomic operations. A race is a program error, but it is misleading to describe Go races as unrestricted C-style undefined behavior; the Go memory model still places implementation constraints on raced reads.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner can state the memory-location, conflict, and happens-before requirements precisely.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: The accesses must concern the same memory location.
At least one conflicting access is a write.
The conflicting operations are unordered by happens-before.
Proper mutex, channel, or atomic synchronization can establish safety.
A data race is incorrect even when the output appears stable.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A data race is a specific memory-model error, not just any surprising concurrent result. It requires conflicting accesses to the same memory location from concurrent goroutines, with at least one write, where neither operation happens before the other. Ordinary read-write and write-write conflicts both qualify.

Happens-before is the ordering Go uses to decide which writes a read may reliably observe. Program order inside one goroutine contributes to it, and synchronization operations connect goroutines. Examples include a matched channel send and receive, observing a channel close, and unlocking a Mutex before another Lock on that Mutex returns.

For example, one goroutine can assign a message and then close a `ready` channel. The main goroutine receives from that closed channel before reading the message. The close is synchronized before the receive that observes it, so the earlier message write happens before the later read.

Mere timing does not establish this order. Sleeping for a second, checking a shared Boolean flag, or assuming one goroutine is faster can still race. Atomic operations are another valid tool when every access follows the atomic contract, but mixing an atomic write with an ordinary read restores a conflict.

Data races are program errors and can produce stale values or corrupt multiword data structures. However, Go's memory model places constraints on implementations, so calling the behavior completely undefined in the C or C++ sense is inaccurate. My practical rule is simpler: shared conflicting accesses need a real synchronization edge, then tests should run under `-race`.

sections.title: Conflict plus missing order creates the race
sections.content: Concurrency alone is not enough, and a write alone is not enough. Identify one memory location, two conflicting operations, and the synchronization path between them. If no happens-before path orders the conflict, the program has a data race.

sections.title: Construct happens-before one edge at a time
sections.content:
Within one goroutine, normal sequencing orders earlier operations before later ones. That local order does not automatically extend to a different goroutine. The `go` statement orders creation before the new goroutine starts, but completion of a goroutine has no automatic synchronization with code that merely continues elsewhere.

Synchronization operations bridge the gap. A channel send is synchronized before completion of its matching receive. Closing a channel is synchronized before a receive that returns because of that close. An Unlock is synchronized before a later Lock on the same Mutex returns. The transitive closure of these edges and local sequencing forms happens-before.

Apply the model to message publication. Worker writes `message`, then closes `ready`. Main receives from `ready`, then reads `message`. Local order connects the write to close, the channel rule connects close to receive, and main's order connects receive to read. The complete chain makes the value visible without a Mutex.

Now remove the channel and replace it with `time.Sleep`. There is no language-defined edge between the goroutines. The program may usually print the expected value on one machine, but the conflicting ordinary write and read remain unordered and therefore raced. Scheduling probability cannot substitute for synchronization.

The memory model also warns about raced maps, slices, strings, and interface values because their representation spans multiple machine words. A read may observe inconsistent component values. Race-free programs receive the much stronger guarantee of sequentially consistent interleaving, which is why eliminating the race is more important than reasoning about a particular observed output.

sections.title: A synchronization chain publishes data
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  W[Worker writes message] -->|sequenced before| C[Worker closes ready]
  C -->|synchronized before| R[Main receives closed ready]
  R -->|sequenced before| P[Main reads message]
  W == happens before ==> P
```

sections.title: Publish a value by closing a channel
sections.content:
```go
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	ready := make(chan struct{})
	message := ""

	go func() {
		message = "safely published"
		close(ready)
	}()

	<-ready
	fmt.Println(message)
}
```
The close-and-receive edge publishes the earlier write. Replacing the receive with a sleep would remove that guarantee.

questions.question: Why does counter++ cause a data race, and how can you fix it?
questions.title: Why counter++ is not an atomic update
questions.direct_answer: counter++ performs a read, arithmetic operation, and write; it is not one atomic synchronization event. Concurrent increments can conflict and lose updates. Protect the operation with a Mutex, use an appropriate sync/atomic type for an independent counter, or send increments to one owning goroutine. Every access to that state must follow the chosen rule, including reads.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner understands compound operations and can choose a valid synchronization strategy.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Two increments can read the same old value and lose one update.
A Mutex protects compound state and multi-field invariants.
sync/atomic fits a simple independent numeric counter.
Do not mix atomic and ordinary access to the same shared value.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`counter++` looks like one source statement, but its effect includes reading the current value, calculating the next value, and writing it back. Ordinary Go operations do not make that sequence indivisible or establish synchronization with another goroutine.

If two goroutines execute it concurrently, both may read 10, both compute 11, and both write 11. One increment disappears. More importantly, the conflicting unsynchronized accesses form a data race, so repeatedly getting the expected total in a test does not make the code correct.

A Mutex is the general repair. Put Lock and Unlock around the complete update and use the same lock for reads. It works for a single counter and also for relationships such as count plus last-updated time. A channel-owner design is another option when increments naturally arrive as messages.

For a standalone metric whose only operations are atomic load and increment, `atomic.Int64` is concise. For example, many goroutines can call `count.Add(1)`, then the waiting goroutine can use `count.Load()`. All accesses to that shared count stay within the atomic API.

I choose from the state rule rather than the shortest line. Atomics are not a replacement for a lock around a multi-step invariant, and WaitGroup only establishes completion with the waiter. The fix is complete when every conflicting access follows one synchronization strategy and a race-enabled test exercises the concurrent path.

sections.title: One line can contain several memory operations
sections.content: Source-level brevity does not imply atomicity. Read-modify-write operations need one synchronization mechanism around the whole transition. The suitable mechanism depends on whether the state is one independent word, a larger invariant, or a stream of owned commands.

sections.title: Compare the three safe ownership models
sections.content:
In the lost-update timeline, goroutine A reads 10 and pauses. Goroutine B also reads 10, writes 11, and finishes. A resumes and writes its already-computed 11. The final value is plausible but wrong, and the memory accesses are raced because no ordering edge connects them.

A Mutex turns the entire read-modify-write sequence into one critical section. It is the default choice when an update checks conditions, changes several fields, or must be paired with a consistent snapshot. The lock's visibility rule also makes previous writes observable to the next holder.

Typed atomic values such as `atomic.Int64` provide operations that are indivisible and sequentially consistent. They work well for independent counters, flags, and pointers with a deliberately small state machine. Once correctness depends on two values changing together, separate atomic operations can expose an intermediate combination and a Mutex is usually clearer.

A channel-owner model removes concurrent access instead of locking it. Workers send increment messages, and one goroutine alone changes the counter. This can fit an event loop or pipeline, but it introduces lifecycle, buffering, and shutdown decisions. It is not automatically better than a two-line Mutex critical section.

Whichever model is selected, mixing access styles breaks the proof. An atomic Add followed by an ordinary read from another goroutine is not a fully atomic design. A protected writer plus an unprotected reader is still raced. Encapsulate the value so its API exposes only the chosen operations, then verify the real workload with the race detector.

sections.title: Choose a complete synchronization rule
sections.content:
| State shape | Strong first choice | Key boundary |
|---|---|---|
| Independent integer metric | `atomic.Int64` | Every access stays atomic |
| Multi-step or multi-field invariant | `sync.Mutex` | Check and update under one lock |
| Stream of ownership-changing commands | Channel owner | One goroutine alone mutates state |
| Task completion only | `sync.WaitGroup` | Does not protect the counter |

questions.question: What is the difference between a data race and a race condition?
questions.title: Data race versus race condition
questions.direct_answer: A data race is the Go memory model's precise case of unordered conflicting memory accesses. A race condition is a broader logic defect in which correctness depends on the timing or ordering of concurrent events. Code can have a race condition without a data race—for example, a locked check followed later by a separately locked update. Eliminating data races is necessary, but invariants must also be atomic at the application level.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner separates memory safety from higher-level timing-dependent correctness.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Data race is a formally defined conflicting-memory-access error.
Race condition is a broader timing-dependent logic failure.
A program can be data-race-free and still have a race condition.
Lock the complete check-and-update invariant, not each line separately.
The race detector finds data races, not every concurrency bug.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A data race has a narrow technical definition: concurrent goroutines make conflicting accesses to the same memory location, at least one access writes, and no happens-before relationship orders them. Go's race detector is designed to report executions that contain this kind of conflict.

A race condition is broader. It means the program's valid result depends on which event wins a timing contest. The individual memory accesses may all be synchronized correctly, so a race condition does not necessarily produce a race-detector warning.

Consider an inventory API. One method locks, reads stock as one, unlocks, and returns true. Later, another method locks and decrements. Two callers can both pass the first check before either decrements. There is no unsynchronized memory access, but the separated check-and-act workflow can sell the last item twice.

The fix is to make `Reserve` one protected operation: lock, check stock, decrement if available, and return the result before unlocking. That preserves the business invariant as one transition. A database implementation may need a transaction or conditional update for the same reason.

I therefore use two reviews. First, every conflicting memory access needs synchronization and must pass realistic `-race` runs. Second, every application invariant needs a clearly atomic decision boundary. Race freedom gives reliable memory semantics, but it does not prove that a multi-step concurrent workflow is logically correct.

sections.title: Memory correctness and business correctness are different layers
sections.content: The data-race question asks whether reads and writes are ordered. The race-condition question asks whether the whole outcome remains correct under every legal ordering. Synchronization can answer the first while a split business operation still fails the second.

sections.title: Concept guide · Data race versus race condition
sections.content:
Suppose `Available` locks inventory, checks that stock is positive, and unlocks. `TakeOne` later locks again and decrements. Every field access uses the Mutex, so there is no conflicting ordinary access outside the guard. The memory model is satisfied for those operations.

Now run two buyers. Buyer A calls Available and sees one. Buyer B calls Available and also sees one because neither has decremented yet. Both proceed to TakeOne. The final stock or number of accepted orders violates the requirement even though the lock prevented simultaneous field access.

The invariant is not 'each read and write is isolated.' It is 'accept an order only if the same atomic operation consumes available stock.' `Reserve` must keep the check and decrement inside one critical section and return whether it succeeded. That method becomes the only public mutation path.

Similar errors appear in files, databases, and distributed services. A transaction with separate read and write statements may need row locking or a conditional update. A deduplication check followed by a later insert needs a uniqueness constraint. The exact mechanism changes, but the check-and-act boundary remains the lesson.

Testing needs both tools. Race-enabled execution detects memory-access violations on paths that run. High-contention invariant tests launch many callers and assert totals, uniqueness, or conservation after completion. Model checking or stress runs may reveal rare orderings, but the strongest repair is an API whose operation matches the invariant directly.

sections.title: Two safe reads can still form one unsafe workflow
sections.content:
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant A as Buyer A
  participant I as Inventory
  participant B as Buyer B
  A->>I: Available locks, sees 1, unlocks
  B->>I: Available locks, sees 1, unlocks
  A->>I: TakeOne
  B->>I: TakeOne
  Note over A,B: No data race, but the check-and-act invariant is broken
```
